clinicalPearls: A neurotoxic syndrome from excess manganese exposure, classically in welders, miners, smelters and battery workers
Also occurs with chronic liver failure (impaired biliary excretion) and prolonged parenteral nutrition, particularly in infants
Produces an extrapyramidal, parkinsonism-like picture that is often poorly responsive to levodopa
Early features include behavioural change, irritability and psychiatric symptoms (historically termed manganese madness)
A characteristic gait with retropulsion and dystonia (cock-walk) may develop
MRI classically shows symmetrical high signal in the basal ganglia (globus pallidus) on T1-weighted images
Management focuses on removing the exposure source; chelation has limited benefit
reference.pathophysiology: Manganese is an essential trace element normally regulated by intestinal absorption and biliary excretion. Excess exposure, or reduced clearance in liver failure, allows accumulation in the brain, especially the basal ganglia and globus pallidus, where manganese is paramagnetic and produces the characteristic T1 hyperintensity. Accumulated manganese impairs mitochondrial function, promotes oxidative stress and disrupts dopaminergic and other neurotransmitter systems, producing an extrapyramidal movement disorder distinct from idiopathic Parkinson's disease and typically levodopa-unresponsive.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of basal ganglia T1 hyperintensity (chronic liver disease, parenteral nutrition)
Progressive supranuclear palsy and other atypical parkinsonism
additionalInvestigations: Whole-blood manganese concentration (imperfect marker of brain burden)
Brain MRI looking for symmetrical pallidal T1 hyperintensity
Review of parenteral nutrition manganese content where relevant
redFlags: Infant on long-term parenteral nutrition with neurological change
reference.prognosis: Neurological deficits may stabilise or partially improve after exposure ceases but can be persistent or progressive; early recognition and source removal give the best outcome.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as idiopathic Parkinson's disease and expecting a levodopa response
Overlooking parenteral nutrition or chronic liver disease as non-occupational sources
Relying on blood manganese alone, which correlates poorly with brain accumulation
Failing to take an occupational history
management: Identify and remove the source of exposure, whether occupational, by reducing manganese content of parenteral nutrition, or by treating the underlying liver failure impairing biliary excretion
Consider chelation therapy such as calcium disodium EDTA to enhance urinary excretion, recognising limited neurological benefit
Trial levodopa while noting the extrapyramidal syndrome is often poorly responsive, and treat parkinsonism and dystonia symptomatically
Manage hepatic dysfunction contributing to impaired manganese clearance
Provide psychiatric and behavioural support for irritability and mood disturbance
Implement occupational health measures with workplace exposure limits and biological monitoring
Follow up with neurology and toxicology, monitoring whole-blood manganese and pallidal signal on brain MRI
